subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Black Death & the Peasants' Revolt
subtitle: The catastrophic plague of 1348–1350 and the social upheaval that followed.

data.targetWord: a serious infectious disease that spreads rapidly and causes widespread death

examples.en-GB: The Black Death was a form of plague that devastated Europe in the fourteenth century.

data.targetWord: a disease outbreak that spreads across many countries or continents at the same time

examples.en-GB: The Black Death was a pandemic that killed millions across Asia, the Middle East and Europe.

data.targetWord: a medieval theory that disease was caused by bad or poisoned air from rotting matter

examples.en-GB: Medieval doctors believed miasma caused plague, so they burned herbs to clean the air.

data.targetWord: the belief that the positions of stars and planets influence events on Earth, including disease

examples.en-GB: Some medieval physicians used astrology to explain why plague struck particular towns.

data.targetWord: a situation where there are not enough workers available to meet the demand for labour

examples.en-GB: The Black Death created a labour shortage because so many workers had died.

data.targetWord: a law passed in 1351 that tried to keep wages at pre-plague levels and prevent workers from moving freely for better pay

examples.en-GB: The Statute of Labourers angered workers who felt entitled to higher wages after the Black Death.

data.targetWord: a tax charged per person regardless of wealth, introduced in 1377, 1379 and 1380 under Richard II

examples.en-GB: The poll tax was deeply unpopular because poorer people paid a similar amount to wealthier ones.

data.targetWord: an unfree peasant legally tied to a lord's manor, who owed labour services and payments

examples.en-GB: A villein could not leave the manor or marry without permission from the lord.

data.targetWord: the feudal system in which villeins were legally unfree and owed labour and dues to their lord

examples.en-GB: Rebels in 1381 demanded an end to villeinage and the right to work for wages.

data.targetWord: a lord's estate consisting of land, villages and a court, which was the basic unit of rural society in medieval England

examples.en-GB: Villeins were bound to the manor and had to work on the lord's land.

data.targetWord: an organised uprising in which people challenge authority and demand change

examples.en-GB: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 saw thousands of rebels march on London.

data.targetWord: a painful swelling of the lymph nodes that was one of the main symptoms of bubonic plague

examples.en-GB: Buboes appeared in the groin, armpit or neck of plague victims and were often fatal.

data.targetWord: the bacterium identified by modern science as the cause of bubonic and pneumonic plague

examples.en-GB: Modern historians link the Black Death to Yersinia pestis, spread partly through fleas on rodents.

data.targetWord: the leader of the Kentish rebels in 1381 who presented demands to King Richard II and was killed at Smithfield

examples.en-GB: Wat Tyler's death at Smithfield was a turning point that helped the government regain control.

data.targetWord: a radical preacher who challenged social inequality and encouraged people to question the injustice of villeinage

examples.en-GB: John Ball's preaching gave the Peasants' Revolt a religious and moral argument against hierarchy.

data.targetWord: King of England from 1377 who faced the Peasants' Revolt as a teenager and later withdrew the promises he had made to rebels

examples.en-GB: Richard II met the rebels at Mile End and appeared to agree to their demands.

data.targetWord: the place where Richard II met rebel leaders on 14 June 1381 and appeared to agree to end villeinage

examples.en-GB: At Mile End, the king's apparent concessions led some rebels to return home.

data.targetWord: the location in London where Wat Tyler was killed during a meeting with Richard II on 15 June 1381

examples.en-GB: After Wat Tyler's death at Smithfield, the Peasants' Revolt quickly lost direction.

data.targetWord: a port in Dorset believed to be one of the first places in England where the Black Death arrived in 1348

examples.en-GB: Trade ships entering Melcombe Regis may have carried the plague to England.

data.targetWord: the isolation of people or places believed to carry disease in order to prevent its spread

examples.en-GB: Some medieval communities tried quarantine-like measures to keep plague away from healthy people.

data.targetWord: a medieval medical treatment in which blood was removed from the body to restore the balance of humours

examples.en-GB: Bloodletting was a common medieval remedy, though it often weakened patients further.

data.targetWord: a result or effect that follows from an event or action

examples.en-GB: One long-term consequence of the Black Death was the gradual decline of villeinage.

data.targetWord: a historian's evidence-based explanation or argument about the past, which may differ from other historians' views

examples.en-GB: Historians offer different interpretations of whether the Peasants' Revolt was a success or a failure.

data.targetWord: a system in which unfree peasants are legally tied to land or a lord, with limited rights and freedoms

examples.en-GB: The Peasants' Revolt was partly a protest against serfdom and the restrictions of villeinage.

data.targetWord: the four bodily fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — whose balance medieval medicine believed determined health

examples.en-GB: Medieval doctors tried to restore the balance of humours by prescribing rest, diet and bloodletting.

data.title: Order the events of the Black Death and its consequences
items: 1347 — Plague reaches Mediterranean ports via trade routes
1348 — Black Death arrives in England through southern ports
1348–1349 — Plague spreads across England causing massive population loss
1351 — Statute of Labourers passed to control wages
1360s–1370s — Further plague outbreaks slow population recovery

data.title: Order the key events of the Peasants' Revolt 1381
items: May 1381 — Resistance to poll tax collection breaks out in Essex and Kent
Early June 1381 — Rebels march towards London under Wat Tyler's leadership
14 June 1381 — Richard II meets rebels at Mile End and appears to agree to demands
15 June 1381 — Wat Tyler is killed at Smithfield; Richard II addresses the crowd
Late June 1381 — Government crushes remaining revolts and cancels promises

data.title: Order the cause-consequence chain from Black Death to Peasants' Revolt
items: Black Death kills a large proportion of England's population in 1348–49
Labour shortage develops as fewer workers survive
Workers demand higher wages and better conditions
Statute of Labourers 1351 attempts to keep wages at pre-plague levels
Poll taxes of 1377, 1379 and 1380 add further economic pressure leading to revolt
